# Self-Authored Direction

> If direction isn't provided from above, you have to produce it yourself. The cost of waiting is constant fire-fighting; the cost of authoring it is the work of choosing.

## Why it matters

In a role where leadership doesn't hand down explicit weekly objectives, the absence of structure is mistaken for freedom. It isn't. It's an open door for everyone else's priorities to walk in and fill the vacuum. Without self-authored direction, the day shape is dictated by the inbox: meetings to schedule, emails to reply to, sponsorships to discuss, partnerships to chase. None of that is *bad* — but none of it ladders up to a stated objective unless you do the laddering.

The discipline is: **daily intentions feed weekly priorities feed department objectives**. Break the chain at any link and you're running around like chickens with your heads cut off.

## Evidence / origin

- Friday 2026-05-22 morning briefing: 5 emails needing reply, 3 meetings to schedule, 1 form owed, 1 FYI — *all* externally initiated. None framed by a stated weekly objective.
- Self-observation during the [[2026-05-22-interview]]: "I can get led astray. Not everything is important."
- The Aranda practice-planning meeting [[2026-05-22_PreSummer_Planning]] is the *same dynamic at the team level* — the head coach is now imposing a deliberate practice framework (green/yellow/red days) so the season isn't driven by whatever the day happens to throw at the staff.
- 2026-06-02 [[2026-06-02-interview]]: "a lot of really talented people who need better, stronger direction so we can achieve some really cool things." The bottleneck isn't talent — it's direction, and supplying it is the unit's job.
=== the-daily-on-ramp.md
---
type: permanent
created: 2026-06-02
source: [[2026-06-02-interview]]
domain: [methodology, decision-making, personal]
tags: [focus, momentum, priorities, OKRs, routine]
status: seed
---

# The Daily On-Ramp

> Self-authored direction doesn't fail at the strategy layer — it fails at the daily on-ramp. The cheap fix is a standing morning brief: *what didn't get done yesterday → what must get done today → the week's big rocks.* That's the mechanism that converts authored direction into daily momentum.

## Why it matters

You can have a sharp set of objectives and still lose the day. The gap between "I know my priorities" and "I worked my priorities" is the first 15 minutes after the workstation boots. Without a deliberate on-ramp, the inbox sets the agenda and good intentions get back-filled by whatever arrives first — and things fall through the cracks not because they were forgotten in principle but because nothing re-surfaced them at the start of the day.

The brief is small on purpose. Three moves — yesterday's incompletes, today's must-dos, the week's big rocks — make the daily→weekly→quarterly ladder *visible at the moment of choosing*, which is the only moment it can change behavior. It's the daily counterpart to the weekly OKR check-in: the check-in sets the week, the brief spends it.

## Evidence / origin

- [[2026-06-02-interview]]: surprised by how little progress a Tuesday produced; named the fix as a morning brief that runs from yesterday's incompletes to today's must-dos to the week's big rocks, "so there's constant momentum and things don't fall through the cracks."
- Directly answers the open question left in [[self-authored-direction]]: *which workflow makes daily → weekly → department traceability cheap enough to maintain?*
- A partial scaffold already exists in the vault (`morning-briefings/`); the insight is to make it a disciplined daily ritual that explicitly ladders to the week's big rocks, not just a list.

=== waiting-for-the-ask-kills-the-idea.md
---
type: permanent
created: 2026-07-29
source: [[2026-07-29-interview]]
domain: [decision-making, leadership, personal]
tags: [process, scope, initiative, permission, resistance, role-clarity, standards]
status: seed
---

# Waiting for the Ask Kills the Idea

> When the expectation to act unasked is real but unstated, waiting for permission looks like professional courtesy and functions as decay. The idea doesn't wait — it expires. The gate is self-imposed, and the cost of holding it is paid in ideas, not in relationships.

## Why it matters

The restraint has a good disguise. "I don't want to overstep or interfere with someone else's task" is indistinguishable, from the inside, from respect for other people's lanes — and it *is* that, some of the time. What makes it a gate rather than a courtesy is who installed it: nobody asked for the deference, and no one is going to issue the invitation that would release it. The expectation running in the other direction — that things get done without being asked — was never said out loud either. Two unstated positions facing each other, and the idea sits between them until it's dead.

This is Pressfield's Resistance in its most respectable costume. Resistance rarely presents as laziness; it presents as a reason, and the best reasons are the ethical ones. "It's not my place" is more durable than "I don't feel like it" precisely because it can't be argued with — it sounds like character.

The asymmetry that settles it: overstepping produces a *correctable, visible* error — someone tells you, you adjust, the relationship holds. Not acting produces an *invisible* loss with no feedback signal at all. Nobody reports the idea that withered. So the cautious path is only cautious on one ledger, and it's the ledger that gets read.

This also completes a gap in [[process-is-the-invariant]], which asked where the line falls between holding a standard and doing invisible work. Part of the answer: a standard held silently, gated on an invitation that isn't coming, isn't invisible work — it's uncommenced work.

**Planning is the gate's second costume.** More preparation is the one delay that never has to justify itself — it reads as diligence, it produces the feeling of progress, and it can be extended indefinitely without anyone calling it avoidance. Confirmed firsthand rather than inferred (2026-07-29): *"Planning can definitely stand in for the build and not really feeding it."* Which makes the same-day essay seed — *"spend a little more time planning things out"* — advice that has to be held carefully. It's correct when the hopper is full and the block is the build; it's Resistance when the block is the ask.

# Finish one project before you start the next one

> The problem was never only choosing the main thing. It is starting the next thing before the current one is finished. Picking priorities without a rule about finishing leaves a pile of started work and little that ships.

## Why it matters

Three earlier notes named the same pain from the choosing side: author your own direction, run a daily on-ramp, keep the main thing the main thing. Four months later the realization is the same, which says the gap is not in knowing what matters. The gap is at the moment a new project shows up while an old one is still open. A self-directed role has no one to say "not yet," so the rule has to be part of the process.

## Evidence / origin

- [[2026-09-14-interview]], essay seed, verbatim: "Finish one project before you start the next one."
- Same day: "I try to take on too many projects and I don't really finish anything before I attempt to take on the next one. I need to develop a system to prioritize my work. Since I am largely self directed I would benefit greatly from having a true process to follow."
- Same day, spent time sorting recent projects into the ones that move the needle: education, analytics, research.
- "I have been on a long pursuit to improve my productivity and figure out how I can provide value. I have had little success thus far."

## Connections
- [[self-authored-direction]] — 5/22: the chain from daily intentions to department objectives; this note adds the missing rule about finishing
- [[the-daily-on-ramp]] — 6/2: the morning brief; it surfaces unfinished work but did not stop new starts
- [[keep-the-main-thing-the-main-thing]] — 7/31: expect the pull toward exciting side work; this is the same pull, seen as a pile of open projects
- [[waiting-for-the-ask-kills-the-idea]] — the tension: acting unasked is good, but each unasked start adds to the open pile

## Open questions
- What made the 5/22, 6/2 and 7/31 fixes stop working? (Not answered on 9/14.)
- Why is now different?
- What counts as "finished" for a project in education, analytics or research?
- How many projects can be open at once per pillar?

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/memory-write

# Memory Write

## Outcome
- Fact added to, updated in, or removed from the correct memory tier
- Tier-B caps enforced (2,500 chars for MEMORY.md, 1,375 for USER.md)
- Confirmation: "Saved — will be active from next session."

## Pick the tier first

Ask: "Will this fact still be true and useful in 3 months, across multiple projects?"

**Tier A — `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`** (one file per fact, indexed by MEMORY.md)
- Durable user facts → `user_*.md` (metadata.type: user)
- Stable project conventions / gotchas → `project_*.md` (metadata.type: project)
- Behavioral feedback rules → `feedback_*.md` (metadata.type: feedback)
- External-system pointers → `reference_*.md` (metadata.type: reference)

**Tier B — `~/.claude/global-memory/`** (single capped file)
- Active threads (in-progress work) → `MEMORY.md` `## Active Threads`
- Current env notes (URLs, tool versions, project structure in play) → `MEMORY.md` `## Environment Notes`
- Pending decisions → `MEMORY.md` `## Pending Decisions`
- Durable user profile updates → `USER.md`

## Steps

1. **Decide tier** using the rule above.
2. **Read** the target file in full.
3. **Dedup check** — substring scan; if the fact already exists, skip or update in place.
4. **Cap check** for Tier B — `wc -c < ~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (or USER.md). If over cap, consolidate (merge similar entries, prune stale) before adding.
5. **Write** the change.
   - Tier A: create a new file with proper frontmatter (name, description, metadata.type) and add a one-line pointer to that slug's `MEMORY.md` index. `name:` follows the rule below.
   - Tier B: append under the correct `##` section.
6. **Confirm** in one line: `Saved — will be active from next session.`

## The `name:` field — bare kebab slug

**`name:` = the filename stem minus its leading type token, kebab-cased.** The type
already lives in `metadata.type` and the filename already carries the prefix; repeating
it in `name:` is the third copy.

| File | `name:` |
|---|---|
| `project_automation-cadence.md` | `automation-cadence` |
| `user_sports-teams.md` | `sports-teams` |
| `reference_baylor-house-style.md` | `baylor-house-style` |
| `feedback_project_idea_capture.md` | `project-idea-capture` |

Note the last row: strip only the **leading** token. `feedback_project_idea_capture.md`
is a feedback memory *about* project-idea capture — its name keeps the word `project`.

`[[links]]` target this bare name, never the filename and never a prefixed variant.

This rule exists because it was previously unwritten: an audit on 2026-09-02 found the
corpus split 59 bare / 58 prefixed, which broke 37 links. Both forms look right in
isolation, so without a stated rule the split regrows on every write.

## Actions

- **add** — append (default)
- **replace** — substring match + swap. Preferred over add when updating an existing fact.
- **remove** — confirm with the user before deleting.

## Retrieval — the tiered ladder

When the user asks about past context, decisions, or "did we already…?", climb in order and stop as soon as the question is answered. Do not run memsearch when the answer is already in the injected snapshot.

1. **Tier 0** — scan what is already in context (USER.md, MEMORY.md, today's compiled log). Zero cost.
2. **L1** — `memsearch search "query" --top-k 5`. Hybrid vector + keyword across all indexed paths: Tier A files (including the Windows-machine slugs), daily logs, transcripts.
3. **L2** — `memsearch expand <chunk_hash>`. Full markdown section around a hit.
4. **L3** — `memsearch transcript <session_id>`. Raw dialogue. Last resort.
5. **Fallback** — say "I don't have a record of that."

## Daily compiled logs — read-only

`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/{YYYY-MM-DD}.md` is produced by `claude-memory-compiler` through its own SessionEnd/PreCompact hooks, and injected by its own SessionStart hook.

- **Never hand-edit these files.** The compiler owns them.
- **Never read them eagerly.** Treat the injected snapshot as the source of truth.

## What is loaded at session start

`~/.claude/global-memory/USER.md` and `MEMORY.md` are read once at session start and are a **frozen snapshot**. Mid-session writes persist to disk but only take effect next session — this is deliberate, to preserve the prefix cache. Never load more than the startup set proactively.

## Rules

- Never exceed Tier B caps. Consolidate first.
- Always dedup before adding.
- For Tier A, the slug is the current cwd with `/` and `.` replaced by `-` (so `~` → `-Users-kristinarash`, `~/DEV` → `-Users-kristinarash-DEV`, `~/.claude/skills` → `-Users-kristinarash--claude-skills`). The harness injects the correct slug each session — use that, don't reconstruct it.
- **Write only to the current machine's slug.** Both machines are active as of 2026-09-10: Mac slugs are `-Users-kristinarash-*`, Windows slugs are `C--Users-eric-rash-*`. A fact written to the other machine's slug is never auto-injected here (memsearch still finds it). Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/` so both machines see them.
- Never announce the write mid-session beyond the one-line confirmation. The injected snapshot is frozen — the new fact appears next session, not this one.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/closeout

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.
  - Repos with dirty state you did not touch: commit and push them like any other, and name them in the report so the user knows another session left them.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours.
- Run the dev-docs harvest so repo docs reach memsearch: `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\scripts\harvest-dev-docs.ps1` (Windows). It copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/`, which is on the index list. One line of output; do this after Step 4 so today's STATUS is included.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.
- **Tier A does not cross machines — mirror it or lose it.** Project memory lives under a slug built from the project's absolute path, and that path differs on the Mac and the Windows laptop, so a Tier A file written today is not auto-injected tomorrow on the other machine. Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. Treat Tier A as a fast local cache and the repo as the record. If a fact only ever exists in Tier A, assume the other machine will never see it.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

**Always, in every repo touched (even for light sessions): update `docs/STATUS.md`.** It is the file the next session reads first, on either machine, in any harness. Rewrite the sections in place, keep it short:

- `## Current state` — two to five lines on where things stand today
- `## Next` — most important first
- `## Open questions` — decisions waiting on Eric
- `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

The dated handoff file is the detailed record; STATUS.md is the summary. Do Step 4 before the Step 2 commit so both land in the same push.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what>
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
```

"Clear to sign off" means: every touched repo is pushed (or is a declared local-only repo). If anything is unpushed, the verdict is "Not clear" and the unpushed repo is the one thing blocking.

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

## Rules

- Push every touched DEV repo. Do not leave the laptop with unpushed work; the other machine pulls from GitHub, not from this disk.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.
